name: Sara Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here is confidential, so feel free to tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm lead at Brook Lane, a community farm run by a charitable trust on the edge of town. We've got 90 ewes, 30 pigs, a small herd of 12 dairy cows and about 80 acres of barley, oats and vegetables. I run a team of three staff and whoever turns up from the volunteer list, so my day is half farming and half teaching people how to hold a lamb without dropping it. On Thursdays school groups come, and that's my favourite day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The money, mostly. The trust lives on grants, veg box sales and visits, and our big grant comes up for renewal every March. I write the farm part of the bid, and I've started using a chatbot now and then to tidy my sentences, which my manager Ruth thinks is cheating. I share a rented house with my friend Hannah, who's a nurse, so between us we're fine, but I've only got about three months' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the honest thing: I never thought a chatbot was going to milk Daisy. At the trust I'd say this proves people still matter more than gadgets. Online I'd probably post a photo of the lambs with a dry little caption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my problem. The grant is my problem. If the March bid fails, the trust cuts a post, and as farm lead I'm expensive compared to the volunteers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job, and I'd keep using the chatbot for the bid, because it does save me a Sunday. I'd also start selling fleeces and shearing for smallholders on weekends, maybe 400 extra over the spring. And I'd put that straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, really. I'm relieved, but the thing that worries me was never about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in your head the week before the grant decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check my email about forty times a day. Last March I worked out exactly which bills I'd drop first: the gym, then the car, and I'd ask Hannah if I could pay less rent for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the farm you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, our pig man, is 58 and has a bad back. If the trust cut anyone, it'd probably be him or me, and he'd struggle to find another job round here.

say: A **chatbot** was never going to milk the cows.
People still matter more than **gadgets** on a community farm.
think: My real worry is the **March grant**, not AI.
As farm lead, I'm an **expensive post** if the trust has to cut.
do: **Keep using** the chatbot to save time on the grant bid.
**Shear** for smallholders at weekends for about **400 extra**.
**Put** the shearing money straight into savings.
feel: **Relieved** but **flat**, because the main worry isn't about AI.
S0.quote: I never thought a chatbot was going to milk Daisy.
fieldNote: Her income depends on **grants**, which matters more to her than AI.
She already uses AI a little but is **matter-of-fact** about it.
She thinks of her **older colleague** Tom when she pictures cuts.

steps.text: Keep writing the March grant bid with the chatbot's help
Shear sheep for smallholders on spring weekends
Save the shearing money towards a six-month cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI should free up people's time for the work that matters, not shrink staff. I'd say that at the trust board meeting, politely. Online I'd share stuff from the farmworkers' union about getting a fair share of any savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one helps me a little. The grant bid, the visit bookings and the veg box orders are the boring thinking jobs AI would take, and that's the part of my week I like least. The worry is the trust deciding the office post isn't needed, and Ruth's office job shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI booking and ordering tools properly, maybe a two-day course the trust pays for in the first year. I'd join the union, which I keep meaning to do. And I'd make the case to the board that the time we save goes into more school visits, not fewer staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously alright. It feels like a new tool rather than a threat to my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ruth's job might shrink. How would you handle that with her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. Ruth hates the chatbot, and if the board started talking about her post, I'd want to be on her side. I'd suggest she takes over running the school visits, because she's brilliant with kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots spread more slowly. What about your sheep and pigs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't see the trust buying a robot for 90 ewes when we can barely fix the quad bike. Our visitors come to see people farming. A robot shearing a sheep wouldn't sell a single family ticket.

say: AI should free up time for **real work**, not cut staff.
Workers deserve a **fair share** of any savings from AI.
think: AI would take the **boring paperwork** I like least.
The **office post** might shrink, which hurts Ruth more than me.
do: **Take** a two-day AI tools course paid for by the trust.
**Join** the farmworkers' union in the first year.
**Argue** to the board for **more school visits**, not fewer staff.
feel: **Cautiously alright**, more a new tool than a threat.
S1.quote: A robot shearing a sheep wouldn't sell a single family ticket.
fieldNote: She sees the **thinking tasks** as the dull part of her job, so she welcomes help.
Her concern moves to **colleagues** in desk roles.
She believes the farm's **human purpose** protects it from robots.

steps.text: Take a two-day course on AI booking and ordering tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one moves much faster. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public money for the kind of work robots can't make meaningful: care, teaching, community farms. I'd say it loudly and I'd sign every petition. To friends I'd say it's the biggest thing that's happened in our lifetime and nobody's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the grants worry me most. If AGI shakes the whole economy in 2028, councils and charities lose money, and community farms are the first thing they cut. By 2031 robots could do the farm work too, so the only reason I'd still have a job is that people want to learn from people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder straight away, maybe 250 a month, and cut the car if I could get a lift with Hannah. I'd keep the shearing going for cash in hand. And I'd join a campaign for a public fund for community farms and food education, and write to the council before their budget in 2027.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I can see what I'd try, but the floor would feel shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we might need to think about who pays what in the house if the trust cuts my hours. Hannah's job in the hospital feels safer to me than mine, which is a strange thing to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still have a job because people want to learn from people. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe sixty percent. If the money's there, I think the farm survives as a place for people. If the money's gone, nobody's paying me to teach kids to bottle-feed a lamb.

say: We need **public money** for work like care, teaching and community farms.
Nobody is **ready** for something this big this fast.
think: Councils and charities would **cut** community farms first.
My job survives only if people still **pay** to learn from people.
do: **Save** about **250 a month** and drop the car if possible.
**Keep** weekend shearing going for extra cash.
**Write** to the council before its **2027 budget**.
feel: **Anxious**, with a shaky floor, though I can see what I'd try.
S2.quote: Hannah's job in the hospital feels safer to me than mine, which is a strange thing to admit.
fieldNote: Her risk comes through **funding**, not direct replacement by robots.
She puts her chance of keeping the job at about **sixty percent**.
She can name a **plan**, which keeps her below alarmed.

steps.text: Save about 250 a month from the first month
Sell the car and share lifts with Hannah
Keep weekend shearing for smallholders going
Write to the council before its 2027 budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a slower version of the same thing. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, so let's plan: public funding for places like ours, and training for farm workers. I'd say it at the trust and at the union. Online I'd share our open day and say come and see what people still do best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd have time to make the trust less fragile. The thinking side, the bids and bookings, goes in 2031, but that's not most of my job. The hands-on side could go by 2034, but the point of Brook Lane is people, and I'd spend the five years proving that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help the trust set up a membership scheme, so local families pay 10 a month and we're less hooked on one grant. I'd do a teaching qualification part-time over two years, so I could work in schools or colleges if the farm can't keep me. And I'd keep saving, maybe 150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like I'm getting ready than bracing for a hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do a teaching qualification. Why that rather than something with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen what I'm good at: standing in a muddy field getting a ten-year-old to stop being scared of a pig. AI can write the lesson plan, but somebody has to be in the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the holiday I've been planning with Hannah. That hurts, but it's one summer.

say: Five years is **enough to plan**, so let's plan properly.
Places like ours show what **people do best**.
think: The **bids and bookings** go first, but that's a small part of my job.
I'd spend five years proving a **people-centred** farm is worth funding.
do: **Set up** a **membership scheme** at 10 a month per family.
**Study** for a **teaching qualification** part-time over two years.
**Save** about 150 a month and skip the summer holiday.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in a getting-ready way rather than bracing.
S3.quote: AI can write the lesson plan, but somebody has to be in the field.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her worry into **concrete projects**.
She picks **teaching** as her fallback because it plays to her strengths.
She expects her own job to **change** rather than vanish.

steps.text: Start a part-time teaching qualification within the first year
Skip the summer holiday and save about 150 a month
Help the trust launch a 10-a-month family membership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And finally. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we don't. I'd push the union and the trust to plan for farms that are partly robot and partly people. Online I'd share it with a photo of the school kids, because they're the ones it's about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly relaxed about this one. I'd be 37 when the thinking AI arrives and 40 when the robots do. By then I could be running the trust, or teaching, or both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brook Lane as I am. In the next few years I'd get onto the trust's management side and start the teaching qualification by about 2029. I'd keep shearing for cash and keep my three months' savings topped up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little knot about the money that was always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money knot was always there. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The grant comes up every March whether AGI is coming in 2036 or never. Ten years just means I have time to fix that, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope Brook Lane looks like in 2040?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots doing the muck-spreading and the feeding at five in the morning, and people doing the lambing, the teaching and the talking. If we get that balance, I'll be happy.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if we use it and a **waste** if we don't.
Farms should plan to be **part robot**, part people.
think: I'll be **40** when robots arrive, with time to move up or teach.
The **grant worry** stays the same whatever happens with AI.
do: **Keep working** as farm lead at Brook Lane.
**Move** onto the trust's management side in the next few years.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with an old **knot** about money.
S4.quote: Robots doing the muck-spreading and the feeding at five in the morning, and people doing the lambing, the teaching and the talking.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **plan a career path** rather than a defence.
Her **grant-funded pay** keeps a background worry alive.
She pictures a **balance** of robots and people, not a loss.

steps.text: Keep running the Brook Lane farm team
Start a teaching qualification by about 2029

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the money for places like Brook Lane would vanish before anyone thought about it. What would help is a steady public fund for community farms and food teaching, so we're not living from one March to the next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the volunteers. Half of them come because they've lost work or they're lonely. If lots of people lose jobs, community farms will be needed more than ever, and paid less than ever.

headlineQuote: If lots of people lose jobs, community farms will be needed more than ever, and paid less than ever.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** farm lead at a charity-run community farm with sheep, pigs, cows and crops.
She shares a rented house with her friend Hannah and has about **three months' savings**.
Her steady worry is the **yearly grant**, which matters to her more than AI itself.
She uses AI for **paperwork** now and then and sees thinking AI as more help than threat.
She stays uneasy in most scenarios and is **anxious** only when AGI comes in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because funding for community farms would vanish before anyone planned.
whatWouldHelp: A steady **public fund** for community farms and **food teaching**.
